chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Startup Funding Rounds Work

lessons.title: Pre-Money, Post-Money and Dilution: The Maths Every Angel Needs

children.text: A founder messages you: "We are raising ₹3 crore at a ₹12 crore valuation. Want in for ₹15 lakh?" That sentence hides at least three questions that change what you actually own. Is ₹12 crore the value before or after the new money? Does it include a new employee stock option pool? And how many shares will your ₹15 lakh really buy? This lesson gives you the maths to turn any pitch into a precise ownership number, so you never have to take the founder's headline on trust.

body.text: Valuation headlines are marketing. What decides your ownership is the price per share and the total number of shares on a fully diluted basis. Learn to convert every pitch into those two numbers.

children.text: Pre-Money vs Post-Money: The ₹3 Crore Question
You met both terms in Chapter 1. Here is why the difference matters so much. Two formulas do all the work:

body.caption: Every valuation question in a funding round comes back to these two lines.
"₹3 crore at a ₹12 crore valuation" read two ways

body.text: The same sentence gives you either 1% or 1.25%, a 25% difference in what you own. Founders naturally prefer the pre-money reading; investors prefer post-money. Never assume. Ask, and get the answer in writing on the term sheet.

children.text: You can also work backwards. When someone on Shark Tank India offers "₹50 lakh for 5% equity", they are quietly naming a post-money valuation:

body.title: Decode the offer
body.prompt: An investor offers ₹1.2 crore for 8% of a D2C snacks brand in Indore. What is the implied pre-money valuation, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Implied post-money = ₹1.2 crore ÷ 0.08 = ₹15 crore. Pre-money = ₹15 crore − ₹1.2 crore = ₹13.8 crore.

children.text: Price Per Share: What You Actually Buy

markDefs.definition: The nominal value printed on a share, commonly ₹10 or ₹1 for Indian private companies. It has nothing to do with what the share is actually worth.
The amount an investor pays above a share's face value. It is recorded in a separate securities premium account in the company's books.
A table listing every shareholder, how many shares or convertible instruments each holds, and their percentage ownership.

children.text: Valuations are negotiated in crores, but you receive shares. An Indian private company's shares usually have a
face value
of ₹10, and investors pay far more than that. The difference is the
securities premium
. To see your real position, you need the company's
cap table
and this formula:

body.latex: \text{Price per share} = \frac{\text{Pre-money valuation}}{\text{Shares outstanding before the round}}
body.caption: Always use the fully diluted share count, which is explained in the next section.

children.text: Rebuild KhetSetu's angel round from Chapter 1 share by share:
Before the round:
the founders hold 1,00,000 shares of ₹10 face value. The pre-money valuation is ₹8 crore.
Price per share:
₹8,00,00,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹800. That is ₹10 of face value plus ₹790 of securities premium.
New shares issued:
₹2,00,00,000 ÷ ₹800 = 25,000 shares to the angels, bringing the total to 1,25,000.
Your shares:
₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹800 = 1,250 shares. 1,250 ÷ 1,25,000 = 1%, exactly what the valuation shortcut gave you.

children.text: The ESOP Pool: Dilution Hiding Inside the Valuation

markDefs.definition: Shares set aside to grant to employees as stock options. They count towards total shares even before they are granted.
Counting every share that exists or could exist, including the ESOP pool and all convertible instruments, as if already issued.

children.text: Startups pay part of their team in stock options, so investors usually require an
ESOP pool
. Serious investors calculate ownership on a
fully diluted basis

, counting that pool as if it were already issued. The catch: new investors typically insist the pool is created before their money comes in, inside the pre-money valuation. That way, the dilution from the pool falls entirely on existing shareholders. If you are already on the cap table, that includes you.

Take KhetSetu's seed round: ₹8 crore at a ₹40 crore post-money valuation. Without a pool, you go from 1% to 0.8%. Now the seed investors also require a new ESOP pool equal to 10% of the post-money company, created in the pre-money. After the round, 20% belongs to seed investors and 10% to the pool, so existing shareholders keep only 70% of the company between them.

body.caption: The pool costs you 0.1 percentage points, or ₹4 lakh of value at a ₹40 crore valuation: 0.7% of ₹40 crore is ₹28 lakh instead of ₹32 lakh.

children.text: Put differently, the headline pre-money valuation was ₹32 crore, but ₹4 crore of it is the new pool. For existing shareholders, the effective pre-money valuation is just ₹28 crore.

body.title: Series A with a pool top-up
body.prompt: You own 0.8% of KhetSetu. Its Series A raises ₹40 crore at a ₹200 crore post-money valuation, and the new investors require an ESOP top-up equal to 5% of the post-money company, created in the pre-money. What is your stake after the round?
body.explanation: New money share = ₹40 crore ÷ ₹200 crore = 20%. Existing holders keep 1 − 0.20 − 0.05 = 75%. Your new stake = 0.8% × 0.75 = 0.6%. Without the pool top-up it would have been 0.64%.

body.text: When a founder quotes a pre-money valuation, ask: "Does that include a new or expanded ESOP pool, and how big is it on a post-money, fully diluted basis?" A ₹14 crore pre-money valuation with a large new pool can be worse for existing shareholders than ₹12 crore with none.

children.text: How Dilution Compounds Over a Startup's Life

body.title: Your KhetSetu stake after each round (%, illustrative)

series.label: 10% pool at seed, 5% top-up at Series A

content.caption: Each d is the total share of the company given up in that round, including any new pool created in the pre-money.

children.text: With pools: 1% × (1 − 0.30) × (1 − 0.25) × (1 − 0.1875) = 1% × 0.70 × 0.75 × 0.8125 = 0.4266%, which rounds to 0.43%. Without pools: 1% × 0.80 × 0.80 × 0.8125 = 0.52%. Two ESOP decisions you had no vote on cost you about 18% of your final stake.
Pro-Rata Rights: Paying to Stay Put

markDefs.definition: A contractual right, not a guarantee, to invest in future rounds in proportion to your current ownership so you can keep your percentage stake.

children.text: The only way to avoid dilution is to keep buying. A
pro-rata right

lets you invest in the next round in proportion to what you already own. To hold your percentage, you invest your current stake multiplied by the new money raised. Before KhetSetu's Series A, you own 0.8%. The round raises ₹40 crore, so keeping 0.8% costs 0.8% × ₹40 crore = ₹32 lakh, more than three times your original cheque.

body.latex: \text{Pro-rata amount} = \text{Current stake} \times \text{New money raised} = 0.8\% \times 40\text{ crore} = 32\text{ lakh}
body.caption: Check: your old shares dilute to 0.64%, and ₹32 lakh ÷ ₹200 crore adds 0.16%, bringing you back to 0.8%. This example ignores ESOP pools.

body.title: The price of staying put
body.prompt: You own 0.64% of KhetSetu before its Series B, which raises ₹150 crore. Ignoring ESOP pools, how much must you invest, in ₹ lakh, to keep your 0.64%?
body.explanation: 0.64% × ₹150 crore = 0.0064 × ₹15,000 lakh = ₹96 lakh. Pro-rata rights get expensive quickly, so most angels use them selectively, only for the companies clearly pulling ahead.

body.title: Spot the inconsistency
body.question: A founder's deck says: "Raising ₹5 crore for 20% at a pre-money valuation of ₹25 crore." What is wrong?
options: ₹5 crore at a ₹25 crore pre-money buys about 16.7%, not 20%; 20% implies a ₹20 crore pre-money
₹5 crore for 20% implies a ₹100 crore post-money valuation
Pre-money valuations cannot be quoted in a pitch deck
body.explanation: At ₹25 crore pre-money, post-money is ₹30 crore, and ₹5 crore ÷ ₹30 crore = 16.7%. If investors really get 20%, post-money is ₹5 crore ÷ 0.20 = ₹25 crore, so pre-money is ₹20 crore. The founder has probably mixed up pre-money and post-money, and you should clarify before negotiating anything else.

body.title: Rohit's two term sheets
body.scenario:
Rohit, an angel in Kochi, can invest ₹30 lakh in one of two rounds. Both startups are raising ₹3 crore.
Term sheet A: ₹12 crore pre-money valuation, no new ESOP pool.
Term sheet B: ₹14 crore pre-money valuation, which includes a new ESOP pool equal to 15% of the post-money company.
Rohit's instinct is that B is the better company because its valuation is higher.
body.prompt: Work out Rohit's ownership in each round and what the valuations really mean for the founders. Which reading of "higher valuation" is misleading?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Rohit's stake. A: post-money = ₹12 crore + ₹3 crore = ₹15 crore, so ₹30 lakh buys 2%. B: post-money = ₹14 crore + ₹3 crore = ₹17 crore, so ₹30 lakh buys about 1.76%. As a new investor, Rohit pays a higher price in B and gets less ownership.
2. The founders' real valuation. In B, the pool is 15% of ₹17 crore = ₹2.55 crore, carved out of the pre-money. The founders' effective pre-money is ₹14 crore − ₹2.55 crore = ₹11.45 crore, lower than A's ₹12 crore.
3. So B's higher headline valuation is worse for the founders and costs Rohit more per share. The pool is doing the work that makes the headline look bigger.
4. One point in B's favour: the large pool is already in place, so the next round may not need a big top-up, which would mean less future dilution for Rohit.
5. The lesson: compare deals on price per share and fully diluted ownership, not on headline valuation.

body.title: The first formula
body.explanation: Post-money is simply the pre-money valuation plus the new money raised in the round. Your ownership is then your investment divided by the post-money valuation.

cards.definition: Pre-money valuation divided by fully diluted shares outstanding before the round.
The nominal value of a share, commonly ₹10 or ₹1 in Indian private companies; unrelated to its real worth.
The amount an investor pays above a share's face value.
A record of every shareholder, their shares or instruments, and their percentage ownership.
Counting all issued shares plus the ESOP pool and convertible instruments as if already issued.
Shares reserved for employee stock options, usually created in the pre-money so existing shareholders bear the dilution.
The right to invest in future rounds in proportion to your current stake so you can keep your percentage.

points: Post-money = pre-money + new money, and ownership = investment ÷ post-money. Always confirm whether a quoted valuation is pre-money or post-money.
"₹X for Y%" implies a post-money valuation of X ÷ Y.
Price per share = pre-money valuation ÷ fully diluted shares before the round; the amount above face value is securities premium.
A new ESOP pool created in the pre-money dilutes only existing shareholders and lowers the effective pre-money valuation.
Dilution compounds: final stake = initial stake × (1 − d₁) × (1 − d₂) and so on, with each d including any new pool.
Pro-rata rights let you keep your percentage, but the cost is your stake × new money raised, which grows fast in later rounds.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All companies, people, valuations and share counts are illustrative. Real term sheets can include instruments and clauses that change these calculations, covered later in this course. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a qualified legal professional before investing.
